## Front Matter

### Libraries

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

### Data Set

```{r}
lego <- read.csv("case-study2-data.csv")
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis: Theme, Pieces, Minifigures, and Unique Pieces (Gavin)

### 1. Data Preparation

#### 1.1 Variable Types and Missing Values

```{r}
View(lego)
```

```{r}
## EDA — Theme, Pieces, Minifigures, and Unique Pieces
### Data Preparation
# Convert Amazon_Price from text (e.g., "$19.99") to a number
lego$Amazon_Price <- as.numeric(gsub("[$,]", "", lego$Amazon_Price))
# Check the structure of the variables we will analyze
str(lego[, c("Amazon_Price", "Theme", "Pieces",
             "Minifigures", "Unique_Pieces")])
# Count missing values in our variables
colSums(is.na(lego[, c("Amazon_Price", "Theme", "Pieces",
                       "Minifigures", "Unique_Pieces")]))
```

#### 1.2 Cleaning LEGO Theme Names

```{r}
# Save the original theme names in case we need them later
lego$Theme_Original <- lego$Theme
# Convert theme names to plain ASCII text
# This removes problematic special characters
lego$Theme <- iconv(
  lego$Theme,
  from = "",
  to = "ASCII",
  sub = ""
)
# Remove any extra spaces
lego$Theme <- trimws(lego$Theme)
# Check the most common themes after cleaning
head(sort(table(lego$Theme), decreasing = TRUE), 15)
```

### 2. Theme Analysis

#### 2.1 Number of LEGO Sets by Theme

```{r}
# Count how many LEGO sets belong to each theme
theme_counts <- sort(table(lego$Theme), decreasing = TRUE)

# Display the 15 most common themes
head(theme_counts, 15)
```

#### 2.2 LEGO Theme Prevalence — Word Cloud

```{r}
library(wordcloud)

# Count LEGO sets by theme
theme_counts <- sort(table(lego$Theme), decreasing = TRUE)

# Create clean theme names for the word cloud
theme_names <- iconv(
  names(theme_counts),
  from = "latin1",
  to = "ASCII",
  sub = ""
)

# Create the word cloud
set.seed(470)

wordcloud(
  words = theme_names,
  freq = as.numeric(theme_counts),
  min.freq = 2,
  max.words = 30,
  random.order = FALSE,
  rot.per = 0,
  scale = c(3.5, 0.7),
  colors = c(
    "#1F77B4",  # Blue
    "#FF7F0E",  # Orange
    "#2CA02C",  # Green
    "#D62728",  # Red
    "#9467BD",  # Purple
    "#17BECF",  # Teal
    "#E377C2",  # Pink
    "#BCBD22",  # Olive
    "#8C564B",  # Brown
    "#E6A23C",  # Gold
    "#264653",  # Dark teal
    "#E76F51"   # Coral
  ),
  ordered.colors = FALSE
)
```

#### 2.3 Median Amazon Price by LEGO Theme

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Calculate median Amazon price and number of priced sets by theme
theme_prices <- lego |>
  filter(!is.na(Theme), !is.na(Amazon_Price)) |>
  group_by(Theme) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_price = median(Amazon_Price),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n >= 10)

# Plot median Amazon price for themes with at least 10 priced sets
ggplot(theme_prices,
       aes(x = reorder(Theme, median_price), y = median_price)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2878B5") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Amazon Price by LEGO Theme",
    subtitle = "Themes with at least 10 sets with available Amazon prices",
    x = "LEGO Theme",
    y = "Median Amazon Price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

#### 2.4 LEGO Theme and Amazon Price Distribution — Heat Map

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Keep sets with known themes and Amazon prices
theme_heatmap <- lego |>
  filter(!is.na(Theme), !is.na(Amazon_Price)) |>

  # Group Amazon prices into ranges
  mutate(
    Price_Range = cut(
      Amazon_Price,
      breaks = c(0, 25, 50, 100, 200, Inf),
      labels = c("$0–25", "$25–50", "$50–100",
                 "$100–200", "$200+"),
      include.lowest = TRUE
    )
  ) |>

  # Count sets in each theme and price range
  count(Theme, Price_Range, name = "Count") |>

  # Keep themes with at least 10 sets with known prices
  group_by(Theme) |>
  filter(sum(Count) >= 10) |>
  ungroup()

# Create heat map
ggplot(
  theme_heatmap,
  aes(
    x = Price_Range,
    y = reorder(Theme, Count, FUN = sum),
    fill = Count
  )
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#EAF3F8",
    high = "#145A86"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "LEGO Theme Distribution Across Amazon Price Ranges",
    subtitle = "Number of sets in each theme and price category",
    x = "Amazon Price Range",
    y = "LEGO Theme",
    fill = "Number of Sets"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )
```

### 2.5 Percentage Distribution of Amazon Prices Within Each LEGO Theme

```{r}
# Calculate the percentage of sets in each price range within each theme
theme_heatmap_pct <- theme_heatmap |>
  group_by(Theme) |>
  mutate(
    Percentage = 100 * Count / sum(Count)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Create percentage-based heat map
ggplot(
  theme_heatmap_pct,
  aes(
    x = Price_Range,
    y = reorder(Theme, Percentage, FUN = max),
    fill = Percentage
  )
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#EAF3F8",
    high = "#145A86",
    limits = c(0, 100),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Amazon Price Distribution Within Each LEGO Theme",
    subtitle = "Percentage of priced sets in each price range",
    x = "Amazon Price Range",
    y = "LEGO Theme",
    fill = "Percentage"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )
```

### 3. Pieces Analysis

#### 3.1 Distribution of LEGO Piece Counts

```{r}
# Summary statistics for the number of pieces
summary(lego$Pieces)

# Histogram showing the distribution of piece counts
ggplot(lego, aes(x = Pieces)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 40,
    fill = "#2878B5",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of LEGO Set Piece Counts",
    subtitle = "Number of pieces per LEGO set",
    x = "Number of Pieces",
    y = "Number of LEGO Sets"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

#### 3.2 Relationship Between Pieces and Amazon Price

```{r}
# Keep sets with known piece counts and Amazon prices
pieces_price <- lego |>
  filter(!is.na(Pieces), !is.na(Amazon_Price))

# Calculate the Pearson correlation
cor(pieces_price$Pieces, pieces_price$Amazon_Price)

# Scatterplot of piece count and Amazon price
ggplot(pieces_price, aes(x = Pieces, y = Amazon_Price)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2878B5",
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#E76F51",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between LEGO Pieces and Amazon Price",
    subtitle = "Scatterplot with fitted linear trend",
    x = "Number of Pieces",
    y = "Amazon Price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

#### 3.3 Log-Log Relationship Between Pieces and Amazon Price

```{r}
# Keep observations with positive piece counts and Amazon prices
pieces_price_log <- pieces_price |>
  filter(Pieces > 0, Amazon_Price > 0)

# Create a scatterplot with logarithmic axes
ggplot(
  pieces_price_log,
  aes(x = Pieces, y = Amazon_Price)
) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2878B5",
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#E76F51",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels = scales::label_comma()
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = scales::label_dollar()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "LEGO Pieces vs. Amazon Price (Log-Log Scale)",
    subtitle = "Logarithmic axes highlight patterns across set sizes",
    x = "Number of Pieces (Log Scale)",
    y = "Amazon Price (Log Scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### 6. Additional Data Quality Investigation

#### 6.1 Missing Minifigure Counts by LEGO Theme

```{r}
# Calculate missing minifigure counts by theme
minifig_missing <- lego |>
  filter(!is.na(Theme)) |>
  group_by(Theme) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Sets = n(),
    Missing_Minifigures = sum(is.na(Minifigures)),
    Missing_Percent = 100 * mean(is.na(Minifigures)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(Total_Sets >= 10) |>
  arrange(desc(Missing_Percent))

# Display missingness by theme
print(minifig_missing, n = Inf)

# Visualize missingness
ggplot(
  minifig_missing,
  aes(x = reorder(Theme, Missing_Percent), y = Missing_Percent)

    x = "LEGO Theme",

```

### 7. Predictive Modeling

#### 7.1 Examining Available Variables

```{r}
# Display all variables in the LEGO dataset
names(lego)

# Check variable types and missing values
str(lego)

# Count missing observations for each variable
sort(colSums(is.na(lego)), decreasing = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# Number of sets with Amazon prices
sum(!is.na(lego$Amazon_Price))

# Number of sets with both Amazon and LEGO prices
lego$Price <- as.numeric(gsub("[$, ]", "", lego$Price))

sum(!is.na(lego$Amazon_Price) & !is.na(lego$Price))

# Examine additional predictors
summary(lego[, c("Year", "Ages", "Pages",
                 "Packaging", "Weight",
                 "Availability", "Size")])

# Check how Weight is recorded
head(na.omit(lego$Weight), 15)
```

```{r}
# Keep LEGO sets with a known Amazon Price
model_data <- lego[!is.na(lego$Amazon_Price), ]

# Set a seed so our results can be reproduced
set.seed(470)

# Randomly select 80% of observations for training
train_rows <- sample(
  1:nrow(model_data),
  size = floor(0.80 * nrow(model_data))
)

# Create training and testing datasets
train_data <- model_data[train_rows, ]
test_data <- model_data[-train_rows, ]

# Check the number of observations
cat("Training observations:", nrow(train_data), "\n")
cat("Testing observations:", nrow(test_data), "\n")

# Compare Amazon Price distributions
summary(train_data$Amazon_Price)
summary(test_data$Amazon_Price)
```

```{r}
# Variables used in Model 1
numeric_vars <- c("Pieces", "Minifigures", "Unique_Pieces")

# Calculate medians using training data only
train_medians <- sapply(
  train_data[numeric_vars],
  median,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

# Create an indicator for missing Minifigures
train_data$Minifigures_Missing <- as.integer(
  is.na(train_data$Minifigures)
)

test_data$Minifigures_Missing <- as.integer(
  is.na(test_data$Minifigures)
)

# Replace missing numerical values with training medians
for (variable in numeric_vars) {
  train_data[[variable]][is.na(train_data[[variable]])] <-
    train_medians[variable]

  test_data[[variable]][is.na(test_data[[variable]])] <-
    train_medians[variable]
}

# Replace missing themes with "Unknown"
train_data$Theme[is.na(train_data$Theme)] <- "Unknown"
test_data$Theme[is.na(test_data$Theme)] <- "Unknown"

# Make Theme a categorical variable
train_data$Theme <- as.factor(train_data$Theme)

# Ensure test data uses the same theme categories
test_data$Theme <- factor(
  test_data$Theme,
  levels = levels(train_data$Theme)
)

# Check the results
train_medians

colSums(is.na(train_data[
  c("Theme", "Pieces", "Minifigures",
    "Unique_Pieces", "Minifigures_Missing")
]))
```

```{r}
# Group themes with fewer than 10 training observations
theme_counts <- table(train_data$Theme)

common_themes <- names(theme_counts[theme_counts >= 10])

# Apply the same grouping to training and testing data
train_data$Theme_Grouped <- ifelse(
  as.character(train_data$Theme) %in% common_themes,
  as.character(train_data$Theme),
  "Other"
)

test_data$Theme_Grouped <- ifelse(
  as.character(test_data$Theme) %in% common_themes,
  as.character(test_data$Theme),
  "Other"
)

# Use the same theme categories in both datasets
train_data$Theme_Grouped <- factor(train_data$Theme_Grouped)

test_data$Theme_Grouped <- factor(
  test_data$Theme_Grouped,
  levels = levels(train_data$Theme_Grouped)
)

# Fit Model 1 using the four EDA variables
model1 <- lm(
  Amazon_Price ~ Theme_Grouped + Pieces +
    Minifigures + Unique_Pieces +
    Minifigures_Missing,
  data = train_data
)

# Display regression results
summary(model1)
```

```{r}
# Predict Amazon prices for the testing data
model1_predictions <- predict(
  model1,
  newdata = test_data
)

# Actual Amazon prices
actual_prices <- test_data$Amazon_Price

# Root Mean Squared Error
model1_rmse <- sqrt(mean(
  (actual_prices - model1_predictions)^2
))

# Mean Absolute Error
model1_mae <- mean(
  abs(actual_prices - model1_predictions)
)

# Test R-squared
model1_r2 <- 1 - sum(
  (actual_prices - model1_predictions)^2
) / sum(
  (actual_prices - mean(actual_prices))^2
)

# Display performance metrics
data.frame(
  Model = "Model 1: EDA Variables",
  RMSE = round(model1_rmse, 2),
  MAE = round(model1_mae, 2),
  Test_R2 = round(model1_r2, 4)
)

# Check whether any predicted prices are negative
sum(model1_predictions < 0)
```

```{r}
# Convert Weight from text to kilograms
train_data$Weight_kg <- as.numeric(
  sub("Kg.*", "", train_data$Weight)
)

test_data$Weight_kg <- as.numeric(
  sub("Kg.*", "", test_data$Weight)
)

# Additional numerical predictors
extra_numeric <- c("Pages", "Weight_kg")

# Create indicators for missing numerical values
for (variable in extra_numeric) {

  missing_name <- paste0(variable, "_Missing")

  train_data[[missing_name]] <- as.integer(
    is.na(train_data[[variable]])
  )

  test_data[[missing_name]] <- as.integer(
    is.na(test_data[[variable]])
  )

  # Calculate median from training data only
  median_value <- median(
    train_data[[variable]],
    na.rm = TRUE
  )

  # Replace missing values
  train_data[[variable]][is.na(train_data[[variable]])] <-
    median_value

  test_data[[variable]][is.na(test_data[[variable]])] <-
    median_value
}

# Additional categorical predictors
extra_categorical <- c(
  "Ages", "Packaging", "Availability", "Size"
)

# Group missing and uncommon categories
for (variable in extra_categorical) {

  train_values <- as.character(train_data[[variable]])
  test_values <- as.character(test_data[[variable]])

  train_values[is.na(train_values)] <- "Unknown"
  test_values[is.na(test_values)] <- "Unknown"

  # Keep categories with at least 10 training observations
  counts <- table(train_values)
  common <- names(counts[counts >= 10])

  train_values[!train_values %in% common] <- "Other"
  test_values[!test_values %in% common] <- "Other"

  # Ensure both datasets have the same categories
  all_levels <- union(unique(train_values), "Other")

  train_data[[variable]] <- factor(
    train_values,
    levels = all_levels
  )

  test_data[[variable]] <- factor(
    test_values,
    levels = all_levels
  )
}

# Check missing values in our additional predictors
colSums(is.na(train_data[
  c("Year", "Ages", "Pages", "Packaging",
    "Weight_kg", "Availability", "Size")
]))

# Inspect the prepared variables
summary(train_data[
  c("Year", "Ages", "Pages", "Packaging",
    "Weight_kg", "Availability", "Size")
])
```

```{r}
# Fit Model 2 with additional predictors
model2 <- lm(
  Amazon_Price ~ Theme_Grouped + Pieces +
    Minifigures + Unique_Pieces +
    Minifigures_Missing +
    Year + Ages + Pages + Pages_Missing +
    Packaging + Weight_kg + Weight_kg_Missing +
    Availability + Size,
  data = train_data
)

# Display regression results
summary(model2)
```

```{r}
# Compare training performance
data.frame(
  Model = c("Model 1: EDA Variables",
            "Model 2: Expanded"),
  R_Squared = round(c(
    summary(model1)$r.squared,
    summary(model2)$r.squared
  ), 4),
  Adjusted_R_Squared = round(c(
    summary(model1)$adj.r.squared,
    summary(model2)$adj.r.squared
  ), 4)
)
```

```{r}
# Refit Model 2 without Size
model2 <- lm(
  Amazon_Price ~ Theme_Grouped + Pieces +
    Minifigures + Unique_Pieces +
    Minifigures_Missing +
    Year + Ages + Pages + Pages_Missing +
    Packaging + Weight_kg + Weight_kg_Missing +
    Availability,
  data = train_data
)

# Check the updated model
summary(model2)

# Check for remaining singular coefficients
sum(is.na(coef(model2)))
```

```{r}
# Predict Amazon prices for the testing data
model2_predictions <- predict(
  model2,
  newdata = test_data
)

# Calculate Model 2 RMSE
model2_rmse <- sqrt(mean(
  (actual_prices - model2_predictions)^2
))

# Calculate Model 2 MAE
model2_mae <- mean(
  abs(actual_prices - model2_predictions)
)

# Calculate Model 2 test R-squared
model2_r2 <- 1 - sum(
  (actual_prices - model2_predictions)^2
) / sum(
  (actual_prices - mean(actual_prices))^2
)

# Compare Model 1 and Model 2
model_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Model 1: EDA Variables", "Model 2: Expanded"),
  RMSE = round(c(model1_rmse, model2_rmse), 2),
  MAE = round(c(model1_mae, model2_mae), 2),
  Test_R2 = round(c(model1_r2, model2_r2), 4)
)

print(model_comparison)

# Check for negative predictions
sum(model2_predictions < 0)
```

```{r}
# Step 17.1: Fit Model 4 - Log-Transformed Regression

# Check that all Amazon prices are positive
summary(train_data$Amazon_Price)
sum(train_data$Amazon_Price <= 0)

# Fit a linear regression predicting log(Amazon_Price)
model4 <- lm(
  log(Amazon_Price) ~ Theme_Grouped + Pieces +
    Minifigures + Unique_Pieces + Minifigures_Missing,
  data = train_data
)

# View regression results
summary(model4)
```

```{r}
# Step 19.1: Evaluate Model 4 - Log-Transformed Regression

# Predict log-prices on the testing data
model4_log_predictions <- predict(
  model4,
  newdata = test_data
)

# Convert predictions back into dollars
model4_predictions <- exp(model4_log_predictions)

# Calculate smearing correction using training residuals
smearing_factor <- mean(exp(residuals(model4)))

# Correct predictions for retransformation bias
model4_corrected_predictions <- model4_predictions * smearing_factor

# Function to calculate testing metrics
calculate_metrics <- function(predictions, actual) {
  c(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - predictions)^2)),
    MAE = mean(abs(actual - predictions)),
    Test_R2 = 1 - sum((actual - predictions)^2) /
      sum((actual - mean(actual))^2),
    Negative_Predictions = sum(predictions < 0)
  )
}

# Compare the existing models and both log-model approaches
results <- rbind(
  "Model 1: EDA Variables" =
    calculate_metrics(model1_predictions, actual_prices),

  "Model 2: Expanded" =
    calculate_metrics(model2_predictions, actual_prices),

  "Model 3: Stepwise" =
    calculate_metrics(model3_predictions, actual_prices),

  "Model 4: Log Regression" =
    calculate_metrics(model4_predictions, actual_prices),

  "Model 4: Log + Smearing" =
    calculate_metrics(model4_corrected_predictions, actual_prices)
)

# Display comparison
round(results, 4)
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis: Year, Ages, Price, and Amazon

### 1. Data preparation and quality checks

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

# The supplied CSV uses Latin-1 text, including the one-half symbol in Ages.
# Read a fresh copy so this section can also run independently of earlier EDA.
lego_eda <- readr::read_csv(
  "case-study2-data.csv",
  locale = readr::locale(encoding = "Latin1"),
  na = c("", "NA", "N/A"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

required_columns <- c("Item_Number", "Set_Name", "Theme", "Year", "Ages",
                      "Price", "Amazon_Price", "Pieces", "Pages",
                      "Minifigures", "Unique_Pieces", "Availability")
stopifnot(all(required_columns %in% names(lego_eda)))

# Convert dollar strings to numbers, retaining original strings for auditing.
money_to_numeric <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(gsub("[$,[:space:]]", "", as.character(x)))
}

lego_eda <- lego_eda |>
  mutate(
    Price_Original = Price,
    Amazon_Price_Original = Amazon_Price,
    Price = money_to_numeric(Price),
    Amazon_Price = money_to_numeric(Amazon_Price),
    Year = as.integer(Year),
    Year_Group = factor(Year, levels = sort(unique(Year))),
    Amazon_Observed = !is.na(Amazon_Price),
    Amazon_Status = factor(
      if_else(Amazon_Observed, "Observed", "Missing"),
      levels = c("Observed", "Missing")
    )
  )

# Normalize Ages_6 - 12 to 6-12 and convert 1 1/2 (the half symbol) to 1.5.
# Ages_NA is a missing age recommendation, not an actual age category.
lego_eda$Ages_Clean <- trimws(sub("^Ages_", "", lego_eda$Ages))
lego_eda$Ages_Clean <- gsub("[[:space:]]", "", lego_eda$Ages_Clean)
lego_eda$Ages_Clean <- gsub("\u00bd", ".5", lego_eda$Ages_Clean, fixed = TRUE)
lego_eda$Ages_Clean[lego_eda$Ages_Clean %in% c("", "NA", "N/A")] <- NA_character_

# A '+' label has a lower age recommendation but no stated upper bound.
# Do not replace the absent upper bound with an arbitrary age.
age_pattern <- "^[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)?(\\+|-[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)?)$"
age_parse_issues <- lego_eda |>
  filter(!is.na(Ages_Clean), !grepl(age_pattern, Ages_Clean)) |>
  distinct(Ages, Ages_Clean)
print(age_parse_issues)
if (nrow(age_parse_issues) > 0) {
  stop("Unrecognized Ages labels: inspect age_parse_issues before continuing.")
}

lego_eda <- lego_eda |>
  mutate(
    Age_Min = as.numeric(sub("[+-].*$", "", Ages_Clean)),
    Age_Max = as.numeric(if_else(
      grepl("-", Ages_Clean), sub("^.*-", "", Ages_Clean), NA_character_
    )),
    Age_Format = case_when(
      is.na(Ages_Clean) ~ "Missing recommendation",
      grepl("+", Ages_Clean, fixed = TRUE) ~ "Minimum age (+)",
      TRUE ~ "Age range"
    )
  )

# Order full age labels by their lower bound, then their upper bound.
age_levels <- lego_eda |>
  filter(!is.na(Ages_Clean)) |>
  distinct(Ages_Clean, Age_Min, Age_Max) |>
  arrange(Age_Min, Age_Max, Ages_Clean) |>
  pull(Ages_Clean)
lego_eda$Age_Label <- factor(lego_eda$Ages_Clean, levels = age_levels)
lego_eda$Age_Min_Group <- factor(
  lego_eda$Age_Min, levels = sort(unique(na.omit(lego_eda$Age_Min)))
)

# Missingness across the ORIGINAL variables, with Ages_NA treated as missing.
missing_values <- vapply(lego_eda[seq_len(15)], function(x) sum(is.na(x)), integer(1))
missing_values["Ages"] <- sum(is.na(lego_eda$Ages_Clean))
missing_summary <- tibble(
  Variable = names(missing_values),
  Missing = unname(missing_values),
  Percent_Missing = 100 * Missing / nrow(lego_eda)
) |>
  arrange(desc(Percent_Missing))
print(missing_summary, n = Inf)

# Report potential problems without silently deleting sets or outliers.
quality_checks <- tibble(
  Check = c("Duplicate full rows", "Duplicate item numbers",
            "LEGO prices that did not parse", "Amazon prices that did not parse",
            "Nonpositive LEGO prices", "Nonpositive Amazon prices",
            "Years outside 2018-2020", "Age ranges with upper < lower",
            "Unique pieces greater than total pieces"),
  Count = c(
    sum(duplicated(lego_eda[seq_len(15)])),
    sum(duplicated(lego_eda$Item_Number)),
    sum(!is.na(lego_eda$Price_Original) & is.na(lego_eda$Price)),
    sum(!is.na(lego_eda$Amazon_Price_Original) & is.na(lego_eda$Amazon_Price)),
    sum(lego_eda$Price <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(lego_eda$Amazon_Price <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(!is.na(lego_eda$Year) & !lego_eda$Year %in% 2018:2020),
    sum(lego_eda$Age_Max < lego_eda$Age_Min, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(lego_eda$Unique_Pieces > lego_eda$Pieces, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)
print(quality_checks, n = Inf)

# A reusable summary that handles groups with no observed values.
numeric_summary <- function(x) {
  observed <- x[is.finite(x)]
  q <- if (length(observed) > 0) {
    quantile(observed, c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1), names = FALSE)
  } else {
    rep(NA_real_, 5)
  }
  tibble(
    N_Observed = length(observed), N_Missing = sum(is.na(x)),
    Mean = if (length(observed) > 0) mean(observed) else NA_real_,
    SD = if (length(observed) > 1) sd(observed) else NA_real_,
    Minimum = q[1], Q1 = q[2], Median = q[3], Q3 = q[4], Maximum = q[5]
  )
}

eda_blue <- "#2878B5"
eda_orange <- "#E76F51"
```

### 2. Year

### 5. Amazon: response distribution and descriptive price comparisons

```{r}
print(numeric_summary(lego_eda$Amazon_Price))
print(count(lego_eda, Amazon_Status, name = "Sets"))

ggplot(filter(lego_eda, !is.na(Amazon_Price)), aes(x = Amazon_Price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = eda_blue, color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Amazon prices",
       x = "Amazon price", y = "Number of sets") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplot(filter(lego_eda, Amazon_Price > 0), aes(x = Amazon_Price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = eda_blue, color = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Amazon prices (log scale)",
       x = "Amazon price (log scale)", y = "Number of sets") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Restrict comparisons to the SAME sets with both prices observed.
# Comparing overall means would mix two differently observed samples.
paired_prices <- lego_eda |>
  filter(Price > 0, Amazon_Price > 0) |>
  mutate(
    Amazon_Minus_LEGO = Amazon_Price - Price,
    Percent_Discount = 100 * (Price - Amazon_Price) / Price,
    Amazon_to_LEGO = Amazon_Price / Price,
    Price_Comparison = case_when(
      abs(Amazon_Minus_LEGO) < 0.005 ~ "Same price",
      Amazon_Minus_LEGO < 0 ~ "Amazon cheaper",
      TRUE ~ "Amazon more expensive"
    )
  )

paired_summary <- bind_rows(
  numeric_summary(paired_prices$Price) |> mutate(Variable = "LEGO price"),
  numeric_summary(paired_prices$Amazon_Price) |> mutate(Variable = "Amazon price"),
  numeric_summary(paired_prices$Amazon_Minus_LEGO) |> mutate(Variable = "Amazon minus LEGO ($)"),
  numeric_summary(paired_prices$Percent_Discount) |> mutate(Variable = "Discount (%)"),
  numeric_summary(paired_prices$Amazon_to_LEGO) |> mutate(Variable = "Amazon / LEGO ratio")
) |>
  relocate(Variable)
print(paired_summary, width = Inf)

price_comparison_counts <- paired_prices |>
  count(Price_Comparison, name = "Sets") |>
  mutate(Percent = 100 * Sets / sum(Sets))
print(price_comparison_counts)

ggplot(paired_prices, aes(x = Price, y = Amazon_Price, color = Year_Group)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey35") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(title = "Amazon versus LEGO recommended price",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: equal prices; above the line: Amazon more expensive",
       x = "LEGO recommended price (log scale)",
       y = "Amazon price (log scale)", color = "Release year") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplot(paired_prices, aes(x = Percent_Discount)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = eda_blue, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = eda_orange) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(title = "Amazon discount relative to LEGO recommended price",
       subtitle = "Positive = cheaper on Amazon; negative = more expensive on Amazon",
       x = "Percent discount", y = "Number of paired sets") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

discount_year_summary <- paired_prices |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  group_modify(~ numeric_summary(.x$Percent_Discount)) |>
  ungroup()
print(discount_year_summary)
```

### 6. Additional missingness, outlier, and predictor checks

```{r}
ggplot(missing_summary, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Percent_Missing), y = Percent_Missing)) +
  geom_col(fill = eda_orange) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(title = "Missing data across the original variables",
       subtitle = "Ages_NA is counted as missing; Minifigures NA has ambiguous meaning",
       x = "Variable", y = "Percentage missing") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Does price availability differ by observed set characteristics?
# This is a descriptive selection check, not proof of a missingness mechanism.
amazon_missing_by_age <- lego_eda |>
  group_by(Age_Min) |>
  summarise(Total_Sets = n(), Missing = sum(!Amazon_Observed),
            Percent_Missing = 100 * mean(!Amazon_Observed), .groups = "drop")
print(amazon_missing_by_age, n = Inf)

amazon_missing_by_availability <- lego_eda |>
  group_by(Availability) |>
  summarise(Total_Sets = n(), Missing = sum(!Amazon_Observed),
            Percent_Missing = 100 * mean(!Amazon_Observed), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(Percent_Missing))
print(amazon_missing_by_availability, n = Inf)

amazon_missing_by_theme <- lego_eda |>
  group_by(Theme) |>
  summarise(Total_Sets = n(), Missing = sum(!Amazon_Observed),
            Percent_Missing = 100 * mean(!Amazon_Observed), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(Total_Sets >= 10) |>
  arrange(desc(Percent_Missing))
print(amazon_missing_by_theme, n = Inf)

selection_summary <- lego_eda |>
  group_by(Amazon_Status) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Sets = n(),
    N_Pieces = sum(!is.na(Pieces)),
    Median_Pieces = median(Pieces, na.rm = TRUE),
    N_LEGO_Price = sum(!is.na(Price)),
    Median_LEGO_Price = median(Price, na.rm = TRUE),
    N_Age = sum(!is.na(Age_Min)),
    Median_Age_Min = median(Age_Min, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
print(selection_summary, width = Inf)

ggplot(filter(lego_eda, Pieces > 0), aes(x = Amazon_Status, y = Pieces)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = eda_blue, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Set sizes when Amazon price is observed versus missing",
       x = "Amazon price status", y = "Number of pieces (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Flag unusual response values using the 1.5 * IQR rule; keep them in the data.
# In a skewed price distribution these can be valid expensive sets.
amazon_quartiles <- quantile(lego_eda$Amazon_Price, c(0.25, 0.75), na.rm = TRUE)
amazon_iqr <- diff(amazon_quartiles)
lower_fence <- unname(amazon_quartiles[1] - 1.5 * amazon_iqr)
upper_fence <- unname(amazon_quartiles[2] + 1.5 * amazon_iqr)
amazon_outliers <- lego_eda |>
  filter(Amazon_Price < lower_fence | Amazon_Price > upper_fence) |>
  arrange(desc(Amazon_Price)) |>
  select(Item_Number, Set_Name, Theme, Year, Ages_Clean, Pieces, Price, Amazon_Price)
print(tibble(Lower_Fence = lower_fence, Upper_Fence = upper_fence,
             Flagged_Sets = nrow(amazon_outliers)))
print(head(amazon_outliers, 10), width = Inf)

# Correlations between response and potential numeric predictors.
# Year is summarized as a categorical variable above. Price is deliberately
# absent here because it cannot enter the assignment's prediction model.
numeric_variables <- c("Amazon_Price", "Age_Min", "Pieces", "Pages",
                       "Minifigures", "Unique_Pieces")
numeric_data <- lego_eda[numeric_variables]
pearson_correlations <- cor(numeric_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "pearson")
spearman_correlations <- cor(numeric_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")
pairwise_n <- crossprod(!is.na(as.matrix(numeric_data)))
print(round(pearson_correlations, 3))
print(round(spearman_correlations, 3))
print(pairwise_n)

correlation_plot_data <- as.data.frame(as.table(spearman_correlations))
names(correlation_plot_data) <- c("Variable_1", "Variable_2", "Correlation")
ggplot(correlation_plot_data, aes(x = Variable_1, y = Variable_2, fill = Correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Correlation)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#B2182B", mid = "white", high = "#2166AC",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(title = "Spearman correlations among numeric variables",
       subtitle = "Pairwise available observations; sample sizes are in the table",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1), panel.grid = element_blank())

# Pages versus Pieces was mentioned in the draft but had no matching plot.
ggplot(filter(lego_eda, Pieces > 0, Pages > 0), aes(x = Pieces, y = Pages)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, color = eda_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = eda_orange) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Instruction pages versus total piece count",
       subtitle = "The fitted line is an exploratory trend on the log-log scale",
       x = "Number of pieces (log scale)", y = "Instruction pages (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Minifigures NA can indicate either zero figures or genuinely missing data.
# Keep NA as missing here; do not automatically replace every NA with zero.
# No values are imputed, and no outliers are removed by this script.
```

### Interpretation notes

-   Year is a release-year category. The 2020 sample ends on September 11, so raw counts do not measure a full year of production.
-   Ages are set recommendations, not ages of purchasers. Minimum-age plots combine ranges and '+' labels; the full-label plots preserve that distinction.
-   Amazon price summaries use observed prices. Missingness comparisons help assess whether the priced subset differs from other sets.
-   Positive discounts mean Amazon is cheaper than LEGO's recommended price. The comparison uses only sets with both prices observed.
-   Price outliers are flagged for review and remain in the analysis. Raw and log scales show different aspects of the distribution.
-   Pairwise correlations use different numbers of observations. Their sample sizes are reported alongside the correlation tables.
-   Minifigures recorded as NA can mean either no minifigures or missing data; they are not automatically changed to zero.
-   These are exploratory associations. Formal modeling and a fitted-model generalizability check remain separate steps.
